name: Brow dyeing blonde / bleaching
lead: Brow bleaching lightens the eyebrow hairs, often to blonde or near white, to change the look of the face. People use it to match brows to lighter hair, to soften strong dark brows, or for a bold, editorial look that contrasts with dark hair.[1][2] The same page notes that dermatologist Hannah Kopelman describes the look as either bold or softer depending on the wearer's hair colour.[2]

The lightening works through oxidation: hydrogen peroxide, made alkaline by an additive such as ammonia, breaks down the pigment melanin in the hair. Home kits typically use around 6% peroxide and salon products up to 12%.[3] Brow-specific products are formulated for the area, and hairstylist Ashleigh Marie Rancilio says head-hair bleach is too strong for it.[2] Bleached brows are reported to stay light for about four to six weeks before regrowth shows roots.[2]

The opposite adjustment, tinting brows darker with dye close to the person's hair colour, is also a long-standing option for sparse or pale brows.[1] No clinical trials of brow bleaching have been published. Dermatologists quoted in beauty coverage and the FDA's hair-dye guidance describe the main risks as skin irritation, allergy, thinning hair and eye injury.[2][4]
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent; dyes may contain phenylenediamine [3]

paras: Bleaching removes pigment, whereas permanent dye can darken brows to match hair colour.[1][1] Fashion-focused sources describe bleached brows as appearing on runways, in editorial work and in costume or special-effects makeup, as well as in everyday style.[2]
Bleached hair often turns brassy or yellowish, and toners are used to shift the undertone.[3]
Hair bleaching breaks down melanin through oxidation. Hydrogen peroxide is the oxidising agent, and an alkaline additive speeds the reaction.[3]

In beauty-press interviews, hairstylist Rancilio says the solution should be specifically formulated for brows, and dermatologist Marisa Garshick recommends a patch test on the inner arm and a barrier of petroleum jelly around the brows.[2] Kopelman advises giving brows time to recover between sessions.[2]

Garshick warns that repeated chemical processing can thin brow hairs and that bleach can cause redness or lighter or darker skin patches, which can be more noticeable on darker skin.[2] Getting bleach in the eyes is described as the most serious risk.[2]

The FDA states that coal-tar hair dyes are not intended for eyebrows or eyelashes, that no colour additives are approved for that use, and that dyeing them can injure the eyes. It advises a skin test before each use of hair dye, notes a negative test does not rule out a reaction, and names PPD as the ingredient most often linked to allergy.[4] Reactions to hair colour may not show until hours or a day later; some European dermatologists have cautioned that patch testing can itself sensitise.[3]

card.summary: Lightening brows with peroxide bleach or dye as a style choice; common chemistry, no brow-specific research.
card.note: Chemicals near the eye can irritate or cause allergic reactions.

quick.overview:
Brow bleaching lightens eyebrow hair, often to blonde, for a distinct look. Dyeing can instead darken brows.

No studies of brow bleaching were found in the sources consulted.
quick.mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide with an alkaline agent oxidizes melanin in the hair, lightening it. Dyes deposit color.
quick.risks: Irritation, allergic reactions (including to phenylenediamine dyes), breakage and discoloration are documented with hair coloring in general. The eye area is sensitive.

refs.title: How experts say to bleach your brows

chain: Peroxide oxidises melanin in the brow hairs
Brows turn pale blonde or lighter
Face looks softer or more striking, or brows match lighter hair
angle.text: Bleaching changes brow colour in a single session, so people use it to match lighter hair or to create a high-contrast, fashion-led look. The result lasts roughly four to six weeks until regrowth shows.
